points: The chapter shifts from the communal to the personal. The community's fate may be sealed with the churban, but Yechezkel tells the exiles in Bavel that as individuals they are always empowered to change - no one's personal fate is fixed by their past sins.

'Do I want the death of the rasha? Absolutely not.' Hashem wants the rasha to do teshuva. Bruria showed her husband Rabbi Meir what this means in practice: instead of davening that his tormenting neighbors die, he should daven that they change their ways. Those who love Hashem hate evil - but the goal is eradicating evil, not evildoers.
Teshuva does more than erase the past: the Abarbanel teaches it can catapult a person to become even closer to Hashem than they were before sinning.

The chapter says Hashem will not punish children for their fathers' sins, yet the Torah says He does. The Gemara resolves it: children bear their parents' punishment when they continue in their parents' evil ways - and we are mirrors of our parents, sharing their genes and upbringing, so continuing their patterns is a real pull.

We are masters of our own destiny. Growing up with negative family behaviors does not define us - if anything, it adds responsibility to break those chains. Through the incredible gift of teshuva a person can become completely different.
